prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms brought optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep B015 as a single-part prize and I now hold it more firmly than in round 1. The scientific core is one nameable idea: trapping many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength, where the light shift cancels on the clock transition while Lamb-Dicke confinement suppresses Doppler and recoil effects. That architecture combines the statistics of many atoms with the narrow linewidth of a single ion, which a single-ion clock cannot do. The decisive demonstration is that the idea reaches the accuracy frontier, with fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. Round 1 gave me reasons to trust that claim more: Pearce and Kroll point out that the agreement is between different species (Sr, Yb) and different institutions, tested through fibre and satellite comparisons, so it checks the uncertainty budgets and does not repeat one design. Katori carries the concept and the first strontium lattice clock, and Ye the quantitative realisation, the systematic-uncertainty frontier and the use in tests of constants. Their roles are separable and documented. Six of eight files prefer this, but I am not relying on that count; the independent assessments of originality, credit and maturity agree, which is what matters. I have dropped my round-1 idea that a two-part package should be seriously tried: the three-person limit would force one of the clock laureates out, and Kroll has convinced me that neither B009 nor B030 is mature enough in credit or mechanism to justify that.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains novelty against the 2005 prize (Hall, Hansch) and the 2012 prize (Wineland, Haroche). I take the chair's question seriously and my answer is that the lattice clock is a different physical architecture with its own originating idea, not a refinement of the comb or of the single-ion clock: the comb is the gearbox that counts optical cycles, the single ion is a different way of isolating the oscillator, and neither contains the magic-wavelength condition. That answer is a scientific judgement, and Eriksson, who ranked it sixth for this reason, can reasonably hold that precision metrology has had its share. The second reservation is credit: Lemonde (SYRTE), Lisdat (PTB), Ludlow, Lemke, Bloom, Hinkley and the single-ion work of Rosenband are not covered by two names. I cannot propose a better set within the three-person limit, because adding a third name would require choosing between contributors whose claims I cannot rank from the supplied material. Third, as an instrument-driven advance it is less obviously a discovery of nature than B014; I take this as a real difference of kind but not a disqualifier.

responses.point: Ranks B015 sixth because the 2005 frequency-comb prize already covers part of Ye's route and because the conceptual reach is lower than that of a new class of matter, while accepting that B015 has the cleanest attribution; now prefers B018 (Kane, Molenkamp, Hasan).
responses.response: I accept your point that Ye's comb work belongs partly to the 2005 lineage, and for that reason I would anchor the citation on the lattice concept and the achieved accuracy, not on combs or on clocks in general. I would also argue that the lattice clock is not a continuation of the comb: the comb solved how to count optical cycles, while the lattice solved how to hold many atoms without perturbing the transition, and these are separate inventions. On conceptual reach, I think the topological-insulator story is the stronger case for a new organising principle and I would rank B018 as my second alternative. But you concede that Mele and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposers cannot be fitted, and that the 2016 prize covers neighbouring ground. Those two problems are a larger attribution and novelty burden than the one B015 carries, so I do not move to B018. If the committee wants the topological option, I would rather it settle between Hasan and Xue first.

responses.point: Keeps B014 first as a discovery of nature in the plain sense, with a compact Halzen and Karle credit, and says B015 should be preferred if clean attribution outweighs breadth of discovery.
responses.response: Your last sentence is where I think the committee must decide, and I would say that it does outweigh it here. I agree that B014 is the better answer to the question of whether nature held a surprise, and the diffuse flux is confirmed in several IceCube channels. But the confirmation is internal to one collaboration, KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD are still maturing, and the credit for a collaboration of hundreds, with AMANDA and DUMAND precursors and Kowalski, Klein and Waxman outside it, is a real arbitrary cut. For B015, independent confirmation is between laboratories and species. I would keep B014 as my first alternative and I would not oppose it in a later year, but I do not think this year's prize should be decided by breadth of discovery alone when the credit cannot be defended as cleanly.

responses.point: Prefers B015 with Katori for the concept and Ye for performance, notes that international comparisons make the 1e-18 claim robust, and argues that the lattice clock is a different physical architecture from the 2005 and 2012 subjects.
responses.response: I agree and would adopt your framing of the novelty answer in the citation. On the pending redefinition of the second, I now side with you and Mehlig that the citation should not mention it; it is a metrology-body decision and the prize should stand on what is demonstrated. I also take note of your Boulder connection and think the committee should record it, as the chair asks, without it changing the weight of your support. I would add that the committee has six explicit supporters but it should not read that as an independent check on the science. My own check is the cross-species, cross-institution comparison that you describe, and I would ask that the final citation say so in substance, by referring to the achieved accuracy.

responses.point: Moved from B014 to B015 for the clear originating idea, the compact attribution and the multi-laboratory confirmation, while admitting that B014 is stronger at opening a new observational window and asking whether Lemonde, Ludlow and Lisdat have claims two names cannot cover.
responses.response: I accept the honesty of your admission and I share it. On the other groups, my view is that Lemonde and Lisdat made important independent demonstrations, but those were comparisons and replications of the idea Katori proposed and Ye took to the accuracy frontier, and the committee needs two roles that are credited by concept and performance. I cannot defend that by saying it is obvious; a third name would be the honest alternative, but I cannot choose between Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow or others from the supplied record, and it would dilute the roles. I also share your experimental request that the committee check whether Ye's 1e-18 systematic budget is confirmed by comparison across species and institutions, which is the part of the record I trust most because it comes from outside Ye's laboratory.

responses.point: Moved from B005 to B015, with the caution that the prize should not depend on the pending redefinition of the second and that a field-neutral reader could ask whether this is a physics advance or an instrument improvement.
responses.response: I take your caution on timing and I have changed the wording of my citation to remove the application. On the field-neutral question, I would answer that in atomic physics a measurement that removes a perturbation by design, and thereby reaches an accuracy no method has reached, is physics and not instrument polish: it already tests the constancy of constants and the gravitational redshift across centimetres. But I accept that a reader from another field could weigh this differently, and I do not regard that as an error. I would only add that the support that exists reflects independent reasoning, not familiarity, since the members who moved to B015 gave their own reasons and kept their doubts.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct invention and not a continuation of the 2005 comb and 2012 single-ion prizes; this is a judgement of weight and I cannot settle it for Eriksson.
Whether two names fairly represent the lattice-clock field when SYRTE, PTB, NIST and the single-ion groups made independent contributions; I can find no three-person set I can defend better.
Whether B014 would be the better prize if the committee decides that a two-name credit can fairly represent the IceCube collaboration and rests on the diffuse flux alone.

My own assessment of the cross-species and cross-institution agreement at 1e-18 is from general knowledge of the comparison data and has not been checked against the underlying published values in the supplied record.
statement.conflict_note: I record no personal tie to Katori, Ye or the other credited names on this shortlist, and I have no documented tie to the IceCube, topological-insulator, circuit-QED, trapped-ion or twisted-graphene candidates. I am a theorist in atomic physics who knows the clock community professionally, and I have long-standing collaborations with Anne L'Huillier, Ursula Keller's group, the Lund attosecond group and storage-ring colleagues, none of which involves the credited names. I note Kroll's disclosed stay in Hall's laboratory and Johansson's WACQT role, and I support recording them. I do not judge that either changes my reasoning, which does not rely on their support.
